short conversation that can be played or role-played (dialogue.js).
Writing skills come last, in brief.
The home page routes link to these topics by #anchor, so keep the ids.

pages.title: English for University Studies
pages.metaTitle: Spoken English for University: Orientation, Lectures, Lecturers, Seminars, Group Work, Presentations
pages.description: Brush up your spoken English for university: introducing yourself, asking questions in lectures, talking to lecturers, seminars, group projects, presentations and university offices, with conversations to hear and practise aloud, plus academic vocabulary, assignment instructions and referencing in brief.
pages.keywords: spoken English for university students, academic speaking, English for seminars, talking to lecturers in English, group project English, presentation phrases, academic vocabulary, English for undergraduates Sri Lanka

hero.text: At university, the first test of your English is not an essay: it is introducing yourself, asking a question in a lecture, and speaking up in a seminar. Seven speaking topics come first, each with a conversation you can hear and take a part in.

items.title: Say the phrases
text: Read each phrase aloud twice.

items.title: Play the conversation
text: Listen for the phrases in use.

items.title: Take a part
text: Press a name and speak that person's lines.

items.title: Make it yours
text: Change the details to match your own course.

blocks.heading: 1. Introducing yourself at orientation
text: In your first week you will introduce yourself dozens of times. Prepare two or three sentences: your name, your course, and one thing about you.

rows: Hi, I'm Dilshan. I'm doing a degree in Computer Science.
I'm from Matara, so this is my first time living away from home.
Are you in the same tutorial group?
Shall we swap numbers, in case one of us misses a lecture?

items.title: The first morning
items.setting: Two new students are waiting outside the lecture hall.

lines.speaker: Dilshan
lines.text: Hi, is this the room for the Introduction to Programming lecture?

lines.speaker: Anjali
lines.text: I think so. I'm waiting for the same one. I'm Anjali, by the way.

lines.speaker: Dilshan
lines.text: Nice to meet you. I'm Dilshan. Which course are you on?

lines.speaker: Anjali
lines.text: Computer Science. I'm from Jaffna. What about you?

lines.speaker: Dilshan
lines.text: Same course! I'm from Matara. It's a bit strange being so far from home.

lines.speaker: Anjali
lines.text: I know what you mean. Shall we swap numbers, in case one of us misses something?

lines.speaker: Dilshan
lines.text: Good idea.

blocks.heading: 2. Asking questions in and after lectures
text: Many students never ask a question because they worry about their English. Lecturers are glad to be asked. A short, polite question is all you need.

rows: Excuse me, could you repeat the last point, please?
Could you explain what you mean by *variable*?
A word or idea is unclear
Sorry, could you speak a little more slowly?
Will these slides be available online?
Is this topic likely to be in the examination?

items.title: After the lecture
items.setting: A student waits to speak to the lecturer at the end of a lecture.

lines.speaker: Student
lines.text: Excuse me, Dr Wijesinghe. Do you have a minute?

lines.speaker: Dr Wijesinghe
lines.text: Of course. What can I do for you?

lines.speaker: Student
lines.text: I didn't quite understand the difference between a sample and a population. Could you explain it again?

lines.speaker: Dr Wijesinghe
lines.text: Certainly. The population is the whole group you are interested in, and the sample is the smaller group you actually study.

lines.speaker: Student
lines.text: I see. So if we survey fifty students, they are the sample?

lines.speaker: Dr Wijesinghe
lines.text: Exactly. Good question.

lines.speaker: Student
lines.text: Thank you. And will the slides be available online?

lines.speaker: Dr Wijesinghe
lines.text: Yes, I'll put them up this evening.

blocks.heading: 3. Talking to your lecturer during office hours
text: Office hours are times when lecturers are available to help students. Go prepared: know exactly what you want to ask, and bring your notes or draft.

rows: Good afternoon. Is this a good time?
I'm in your second-year Economics class.
Would it be possible to have an extension?

items.title: Asking for an extension
items.setting: A student visits a lecturer during office hours.

lines.speaker: Nadeesha
lines.text: Good afternoon, Professor Silva. Is this a good time?

lines.speaker: Prof. Silva
lines.text: Yes, come in. How can I help?

lines.speaker: Nadeesha
lines.text: I'm Nadeesha, from your second-year Economics class. I've been ill this week, and I'm behind with the essay.

lines.speaker: Prof. Silva
lines.text: I'm sorry to hear that. Are you feeling better now?

lines.speaker: Nadeesha
lines.text: Yes, thank you. Would it be possible to have a few extra days?

lines.speaker: Prof. Silva
lines.text: Can you bring a medical certificate? If so, you can submit it next Wednesday.

lines.speaker: Nadeesha
lines.text: Yes, I have one. Thank you, that's really helpful.

blocks.heading: 4. Speaking up in seminars
text: In seminars, you are expected to speak. You do not need a perfect idea: agreeing with a reason, asking a question or adding an example all count.

rows: In my view, ... / It seems to me that...
I see your point, but I'm not sure that...
Just to add an example, in my village...
Could you explain what you mean by...?
Could I just come in here?

items.title: A seminar on social media
items.setting: A tutor leads a small discussion group.

lines.speaker: Tutor
lines.text: So, does social media help students learn? Kasun, what do you think?

lines.speaker: Kasun
lines.text: In my view, it can help, because students share notes and ask each other questions in groups.

lines.speaker: Fathima
lines.text: Could I just come in here? I see your point, but I'm not sure it helps most students. It can also be very distracting.

lines.speaker: Kasun
lines.text: That's true. Maybe it depends on how it's used.

lines.speaker: Tutor
lines.text: Good. Fathima, could you give an example?

lines.speaker: Fathima
lines.text: Well, I often start checking a study group and end up watching videos for an hour.

blocks.heading: 5. Group project meetings
text: Group projects succeed when everyone knows what to do and by when. Clear, polite English stops misunderstandings.

rows: Shall we start? Let's decide who does what.
I can do the survey, if that's OK.
How about meeting again on Thursday?
So, just to confirm, you're writing the introduction?
Can we all finish our parts by Monday?

items.title: Dividing the work
items.setting: Three students plan a group presentation.

lines.speaker: Ravi
lines.text: Shall we start? We need to decide who does what for the presentation.

lines.speaker: Hasini
lines.text: I can do the survey and the charts, if that's OK.

lines.speaker: Imran
lines.text: Great. I'll write the introduction and the conclusion.

lines.speaker: Ravi
lines.text: Then I'll prepare the slides. Can we all finish our parts by Monday?

lines.speaker: Hasini
lines.text: Monday is fine. How about meeting on Tuesday to practise?

lines.speaker: Imran
lines.text: So, just to confirm: survey and charts, Hasini; introduction and conclusion, me; slides, Ravi; practice on Tuesday.

lines.speaker: Ravi
lines.text: Perfect.

blocks.heading: 6. Giving a presentation and answering questions
text: Tell the audience what is coming, deliver it clearly, and remind them what they heard. The hardest part for many students is the questions at the end: it is fine to take a moment to think.

rows: Good morning. Today I'm going to talk about...
My presentation has three parts. First..., then..., and finally...
This brings me to my second point.
To sum up, the key message is...
That's a good question. Let me think for a moment.
I'm not sure, but I'll find out and let you know.

items.title: Questions after a presentation
items.setting: A student has just finished presenting a survey on how students travel to campus.

lines.speaker: Hasini
lines.text: To sum up, most students travel by bus, but many would cycle if there were safe cycle lanes. Thank you for listening. Are there any questions?

lines.speaker: Lecturer
lines.text: Thank you, Hasini. How many students did you survey?

lines.speaker: Hasini
lines.text: We surveyed eighty students from three faculties.

lines.speaker: Lecturer
lines.text: And do you think the results would be the same at other universities?

lines.speaker: Hasini
lines.text: That's a good question. Let me think for a moment. Probably not, because our campus is close to the town centre.

blocks.heading: 7. The library and university offices
text: Registering, borrowing books and sorting out problems all mean speaking to staff. Explain the problem clearly and have your student number ready.

rows: I'd like to register for the second semester.
Could you tell me where I can find books on statistics?
How long can I borrow this for?
My student ID card isn't working.

items.title: At the library desk
items.setting: A student needs help finding a book.

lines.speaker: Student
lines.text: Excuse me, could you tell me where I can find books on statistics?

lines.speaker: Librarian
lines.text: Yes, they're on the second floor, in the mathematics section.

lines.speaker: Student
lines.text: Thank you. How long can I borrow a book for?

lines.speaker: Librarian
lines.text: Two weeks, and you can renew it online if nobody else has reserved it.

lines.speaker: Student
lines.text: Great. And my student card isn't working at the entrance gate.

lines.speaker: Librarian
lines.text: Let me check. What's your student number?

blocks.heading: 8. Academic vocabulary, said correctly
text: These words appear in every subject. Learn the meaning, and practise the stress too: the stressed part is in capitals. A word said with the wrong stress can be hard for a lecturer to understand.

rows: facts that show something is true
large or important enough to notice
a way of dealing with something
a planned way of doing something
an idea that a study tests
to decide after looking at the evidence
careful study to discover facts (both are heard)

blocks.heading: 9. Understanding assignment instructions
text: The first word of an assignment question tells you what to do. Students lose marks by describing when the question asks them to evaluate.

rows: Say what something is like, or what happened.
Say why or how something happens, with reasons.
Show the similarities and the differences.
Look at different sides of an issue and reach a view.
Judge the strengths and weaknesses, and conclude.
Give good reasons for a decision or opinion.

blocks.heading: 10. Academic writing in brief: style, paraphrasing and referencing
text: Your department will teach academic writing in detail. These four rules will keep you safe from the start.

parts.heading: The essentials
bullets: **Formal style:** no contractions (*it is*, not *it's*) and no informal words (*children*, not *kids*).
**Paraphrase properly:** understand the idea, cover the original, and write it in your own words and sentence structure.
**Always reference:** any idea or words from another writer need a reference, in the style your department asks for (such as APA or Harvard). Using them without one is plagiarism, even by accident.

pages.title: English for Working Abroad
pages.metaTitle: Spoken English for Working Abroad: Job Interviews, Workplace, Customers, Safety, Telephone
pages.description: Brush up your spoken English for a job overseas: introducing yourself, job interviews, your first days, checking instructions, customers, colleagues, the telephone, reporting safety problems and talking about pay and time off, with conversations to hear and practise aloud, plus CVs and cover letters in brief.
pages.keywords: spoken English for foreign job, English for working abroad, job interview English speaking, workplace English conversation, English for migrant workers Sri Lanka, customer service English, safety English at work

hero.text: Abroad, your English is tested every day out loud: in the interview, with your supervisor, with customers and on the phone. Nine speaking topics come first, each with a conversation you can hear and take a part in.

blocks.title: About this page
text: This page helps with the English you need for work abroad. It is not legal, visa or employment advice. Before you accept a job or sign anything, check official guidance, for example from the Sri Lanka Bureau of Foreign Employment, and the rules of the country you are going to.

items.title: Say the phrases
text: Read each phrase aloud twice.

items.title: Play the conversation
text: Listen for the phrases in use.

items.title: Take a part
text: Press a name and speak that person's lines.

items.title: Make it yours
text: Change the details to match your own job.

blocks.heading: 1. Introducing yourself and your experience
text: *Tell me about yourself* is the first question in almost every interview, and you will introduce yourself again on your first day. Prepare 30 seconds: who you are, your experience, and why you want this work.

rows: My name is Chaminda, and I'm from Galle in Sri Lanka.
I've worked as a cook for three years.
In my last job, I prepared meals for up to two hundred guests a day.
I'm hardworking, and I learn new tasks quickly.
I'd like to develop my career in a large hotel.

items.title: Tell me about yourself
items.setting: The first question in an online interview for a hotel kitchen job.

lines.speaker: Interviewer
lines.text: Good morning, Chaminda. Can you hear me clearly?

lines.speaker: Chaminda
lines.text: Yes, very clearly, thank you. Good morning.

lines.speaker: Interviewer
lines.text: Great. Let's begin. Could you tell me a little about yourself?

lines.speaker: Chaminda
lines.text: Of course. I'm from Galle in Sri Lanka, and I've worked as a cook for three years in a busy tourist hotel. I prepare meals for up to two hundred guests a day, and I always follow food safety rules. I'd like to develop my career in a large international hotel.

blocks.heading: 2. The job interview
text: Prepare answers to the common questions and practise saying them aloud. For experience questions, tell a short story: the situation, what you did, and the result.

rows: Why do you want this job?
What interests you about the work, not only the pay
Tell me about a problem you solved at work.
The situation, what you did, and the result
A strength with a short example
Always ask one, about training or working hours

lines.speaker: Interviewer
lines.text: Tell me about a problem you solved at work.

lines.speaker: Chaminda
lines.text: Once, a large group arrived an hour early for dinner, and half of our kitchen staff had not started their shift.

lines.speaker: Interviewer
lines.text: What did you do?

lines.speaker: Chaminda
lines.text: I spoke to my supervisor, and we started with the dishes that were quickest to prepare. I also called two colleagues, who came in early.

lines.speaker: Interviewer
lines.text: And the result?

lines.speaker: Chaminda
lines.text: All the guests were served within thirty minutes, and the manager thanked the team the next day.

lines.speaker: Interviewer
lines.text: Very good. Do you have any questions for us?

lines.speaker: Chaminda
lines.text: Yes. Is there any training for new staff when they arrive?

blocks.heading: 3. Your first days at work
text: In the first week, nobody expects you to know everything, but they do expect you to ask.

rows: Hello, I'm Kamal. I've just started in the stores department.
What time do I start and finish?
Where can I leave my bag?
Who should I ask if I have a problem?
Could you show me how this works, please?

items.title: Day one in the warehouse
items.setting: Kamal meets his supervisor on his first morning.

lines.speaker: Supervisor
lines.text: Morning! You must be Kamal. I'm Mark, the shift supervisor.

lines.speaker: Kamal
lines.text: Good morning, Mark. Nice to meet you.

lines.speaker: Supervisor
lines.text: Your shift is seven to four, with a break at eleven. Lockers are over there.

lines.speaker: Kamal
lines.text: Thank you. Who should I ask if I have a problem?

lines.speaker: Supervisor
lines.text: Ask me, or Priya on the next aisle. She's been here five years.

lines.speaker: Kamal
lines.text: Great. Could you show me how the scanner works, please?

blocks.heading: 4. Understanding and checking instructions
text: Doing a task wrongly because you were too shy to ask can cost money or cause an accident. When you are not sure, repeat the instruction back.

rows: Sorry, could you say that again more slowly?
Just to check: you want me to clean floor two first?
When you say *urgent*, do you mean today, or right now?
Could you show me once, please?
I've finished. Could you check it's right?

items.title: Checking a task
items.setting: A housekeeping supervisor gives instructions in a hotel.

lines.speaker: Supervisor
lines.text: Sunitha, rooms two-fourteen to two-twenty are checking out early, so do those first, then the rest of floor three.

lines.speaker: Sunitha
lines.text: Sorry, could you say the room numbers again, a little more slowly?

lines.speaker: Supervisor
lines.text: Two-fourteen to two-twenty.

lines.speaker: Sunitha
lines.text: Just to check: rooms two-fourteen to two-twenty first, and then floor three?

lines.speaker: Supervisor
lines.text: That's right. Thank you for checking.

blocks.heading: 5. Serving customers and handling complaints
text: When a customer complains, follow four steps: **listen, apologise, solve, thank.** Stay calm, and never argue.

rows: Good evening. How can I help you?
I understand. Could you tell me what happened?
Let me change that for you right away.

items.title: The wrong order
items.setting: A customer in a restaurant has received the wrong meal.

lines.speaker: Customer
lines.text: Excuse me, I ordered the grilled fish, but this is chicken.

lines.speaker: Waiter
lines.text: I'm very sorry about that. Let me check your order.

lines.speaker: Customer
lines.text: And we've been waiting almost forty minutes.

lines.speaker: Waiter
lines.text: I understand, and I apologise for the wait. I'll ask the kitchen to prepare your fish right away.

lines.speaker: Customer
lines.text: Thank you.

lines.speaker: Waiter
lines.text: Thank you for telling me. I'll bring you a drink while you wait.

blocks.heading: 6. Working with colleagues
text: Friendly, polite English makes teamwork easier, especially in teams where people come from many countries.

rows: Could you give me a hand with this?
No problem, I'll do it now.
Sorry, I can't right now. I'm finishing this job.
Do you want to have lunch together?

lines.speaker: Kamal
lines.text: Priya, could you give me a hand with these boxes? They're really heavy.

lines.speaker: Priya
lines.text: Sorry, I can't right now. I'm finishing the price labels. Can you wait five minutes?

lines.speaker: Kamal
lines.text: Sure, no problem.

lines.speaker: Priya
lines.text: OK, I'm done. Let's lift them together.

lines.speaker: Kamal
lines.text: Thanks. Do you want to have lunch together later?

lines.speaker: Priya
lines.text: Good idea. See you at one.

blocks.heading: 7. The telephone: calling in sick and taking messages
text: On the phone, say who you are first, and speak a little more slowly than usual. If you are ill or late, call as early as you can.

rows: Hello, this is Sunil from the night shift.
I'm sorry, but I'm ill and I can't come in today.
She isn't here at the moment. Can I take a message?
Could you spell your name, please?
Could you repeat the number, please?

items.title: Calling in sick
items.setting: Sunil telephones his workplace early in the morning.

lines.speaker: Manager
lines.text: Good morning, Harbour Logistics.

lines.speaker: Sunil
lines.text: Good morning. This is Sunil Perera from the night shift.

lines.speaker: Manager
lines.text: Hello, Sunil. What's the problem?

lines.speaker: Sunil
lines.text: I'm sorry, but I have a high fever and I can't come to work tonight.

lines.speaker: Manager
lines.text: Thanks for letting me know early. Will you see a doctor?

lines.speaker: Sunil
lines.text: Yes, this morning. I'll call you tomorrow to say how I am.

lines.speaker: Manager
lines.text: OK. Get well soon.

blocks.heading: 8. Safety: signs and reporting problems
text: Learn the key safety words before your first day. And if something is unsafe, say so at once: you are never wrong to report a safety problem.

rows: Serious risk of injury or death
Be careful: there is a risk
Do not go in without permission
The way out in an emergency
Wear the gloves, helmet, glasses or boots provided

items.title: Reporting a hazard
items.setting: A worker notices a problem on a building site.

lines.speaker: Nimal
lines.text: Excuse me, the safety rail on the second floor is loose. I think it's dangerous.

lines.speaker: Site supervisor
lines.text: Thanks, Nimal. Which side exactly?

lines.speaker: Nimal
lines.text: The side near the stairs. Someone could fall.

lines.speaker: Site supervisor
lines.text: Right. Nobody works on that side until it's fixed. Could you put a warning sign there?

lines.speaker: Nimal
lines.text: Yes, I'll do it now.

lines.speaker: Site supervisor
lines.text: Good work. Always tell me straight away, like this.

blocks.heading: 9. Talking about pay, hours and time off
text: It is normal to ask about your pay and hours, politely. Know these words, and never sign a contract you do not fully understand: ask for a copy and take your time.

rows: your pay, often monthly (salary) or hourly (wage)
extra hours beyond your normal hours
money taken from your pay, for example for tax or accommodation
how long before leaving you must tell your employer

items.title: A question about the payslip
items.setting: A worker speaks to the office manager.

lines.speaker: Sunitha
lines.text: Excuse me, could I ask a question about my payslip?

lines.speaker: Office manager
lines.text: Of course. What's the problem?

lines.speaker: Sunitha
lines.text: I worked six hours of overtime last week, but I can't see it here.

lines.speaker: Office manager
lines.text: Let me look. Ah, the overtime is paid next month.

lines.speaker: Sunitha
lines.text: I see, thank you. And would it be possible to take two days of annual leave in December?

lines.speaker: Office manager
lines.text: Please fill in a leave form, and I'll ask your supervisor.

blocks.heading: 10. Your CV and cover letter in brief
text: Your CV gets you the interview; your speaking gets you the job. Keep the writing short and clear.

parts.heading: CV
bullets: Sections: contact details, a two-sentence profile, work experience (most recent first), training, and skills such as languages and a driving licence.
Begin each duty with an action verb: *prepared*, *repaired*, *served*, *managed*.
One or two pages. Check what employers in that country expect, for example whether to include a photograph.

parts.heading: Cover letter or email
bullets: Say which job you are applying for.
Give two or three reasons you are suitable, with real details.
Say that your CV is attached and that you are available for an interview.
